article.heading: Converting between CSV and JSON without a server
article.p1: CSV and JSON solve the same problem — moving structured data between systems — in two very different shapes. CSV is a flat table: rows and columns, nothing more, which is why every spreadsheet app, database export, and legacy system speaks it fluently. JSON is a tree: objects can nest inside objects, arrays can hold anything, which is why every modern API and JavaScript codebase speaks it instead. The moment you need to load a spreadsheet into an API, or turn an API response into something you can open in Excel, you're stuck translating between the two — and getting that translation exactly right (quoted fields with embedded commas, escaped quotes, nested objects that don't map to a single column) is easy to get subtly wrong by hand.
article.p2: This tool runs the conversion entirely in your browser using a battle-tested CSV parser, so the data you paste — which might be a customer export, an internal report, or an API response you'd rather not hand to a third-party website — never leaves your machine. There's no upload step, no server round-trip, and no size limit imposed by a network request; it's the same engine either direction, so a round trip through Swap should give you back what you started with.
article.p3: Pick your delimiter (comma, semicolon, tab, or any custom character — handy for European-locale CSV exports that use semicolons, or pipe-delimited legacy exports), toggle whether the first row holds column names, and decide whether nested JSON keys like `address.city` should become one flattened CSV column or be rebuilt into a nested object on the way back to JSON. Pretty-print the JSON output for readability or leave it minified for pasting straight into code. If your CSV has a malformed quote or an inconsistent row, the parser tells you exactly which row failed instead of silently producing garbage.
article.p4: Drag a file straight onto the drop zone or paste text directly — both work identically. Once you're happy with the result, copy it to your clipboard or download it as a ready-to-use `.json` or `.csv` file. If you need to reshape the JSON output further, or validate it against a schema, the JSON Formatter & Validator is a natural next stop; if you're working with API tokens rather than tabular data, the JWT Decoder and Base64 Encode/Decode tools cover that side of the developer-tools toolbox.
